speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) how do the revised targets for fibre and protein productions by 2035 compare to the "30 by 30" targets in terms of total local food production volume; and (b) how will the Ministry ensure that these revised targets are adequate, sustainable and resilient to current and future challenges.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) what is the rationale for setting targets specifically for (i) fibre and (ii) protein production in the Ministry's new 2035 farming goals; and (b) how is Singapore's food security measured vis-à-vis local farming production.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This has evolved into the Singapore Food Story 2, which aims to bring about overall food resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This ensures that we have sufficient food supply in times of disruption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The revised local production targets take into account the important role of local food production as a regenerative and assured source of fresh food, the strengths of our local farming ecosystem and their potential for growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We will focus on food types that are feasible to be produced at scale efficiently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This is consistently applied in our grants and land tenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Alternative protein is also excluded given the nascency of the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The revised targets balance ambition and pragmatism, by considering what we can produce and scale locally as well as the challenges our nascent sector faces, including higher production costs and the need for substitute demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: To achieve them, we will continue to find ways to support new and existing farms in lowering production costs, building capability, strengthening the supply resilience of inputs and enhancing demand offtake.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The Government will continue to invest efforts in building local production capability and capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Food security is a joint responsibility that requires the nation's collective effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We also need strong support from local consumers and businesses which is essential for our farms to achieve scale and commercial viability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We will provide more information on our support schemes at the coming Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy, I assume you are answering Question Nos 3 and 4?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Yes, Mr Speaker, I was answering Question Nos 3 and 4.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Small farms and food producers form part of Singapore's small and medium enterprise landscape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What concrete job creation or retention targets accompany the new production goals, especially for sectors affected by high production costs and workforce shortages?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that locally produced food often cost more than imported alternatives, how did the Ministry assess the potential price impacts on households, if the revised targets are met?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures are in place to prevent local production from inadvertently raising food prices for Singaporean families?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the past few years, as the Member has highlighted, the global agri-food sector has faced headwinds.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have also faced supply chain disruptions ever since COVID-19 and we have seen how those have impacted us.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This helps our farms build up capability in new areas such as agri-tech.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we have seen farms such as Green Harvest, as an example, who today own several farm plots and already supply to many of our supermarkets, even wet markets as well.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While they have been established over decades, they have also been able to transform.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They set up a joint venture, Green Harvest, together with Team Build Construction.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want to help our farmers transform, because with higher yields, it also means that they can be more competitive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They can provide a different suite of offerings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And certainly, when we think about Singapore's land constraints, where only 1% of our land use is dedicated to farms and farming, I think then, we have to be really smart about how we use our farms to achieve these outputs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Having said that, I am also going to say that I think it is also important that as we look at agri-tech, agri-food, new technology, new capabilities, it also has to overcome some of our constraints.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Energy use, I think, is one area in which some of our new farms are able to overcome – they are now looking at low-energy type facilities, where they can reduce energy costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, automation helps us reduce manpower.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I have spoken about Green Harvest that today already produces about three times the yield of traditional farms.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the extreme end, we also have Greenphyto which just, I think some Members may have read in the news, launched last week, at the cost of about $80 million investment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you can get to somewhere in between, then that, I think changes the game for our agri-food sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I want us to imagine a very different food sector in the near future where we talk about not just food resilience in terms of local farming, but also how we use our other pillars in the Singapore Food Story 2, which has evolved our food resilience narrative.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I have spoken about stockpiling at the last Sitting.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There are also global partnerships, which Members would have probably noticed, some of the recent agreements which have been made.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: More importantly, I think it is really about overcoming our land constraints, but thinking about how we achieve our outputs and productions in a very different manner from where it is today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have three supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first is, given the shift in 2030 target, to 2035, what prevents further deadline extensions if headwinds persist, particularly given the current uncertainty around the geopolitical climate as well?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And my third supplementary question is, given the original "30 by 30" goal was described as aspirational, could I just ask for confirmation whether these new targets are targets or aspirations?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I will start with the third question first, on "30 by 30" and where we are in the Singapore Food Story.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think the Member will recall, it was in 2019 when we embarked on the "30 by 30" vision, where we wanted to grow a local food strategy to build food supply resilience.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That was how we got Singaporeans to really think about food resilience, how we build this story and how we build this narrative of relying on local produce, helping local produce grow and support us in times of difficulty or challenges, when it comes to supply disruptions.
And certainly, even then, we had some forms of the other pillars, which is stockpiling and others.
Since 2019, we have gone through several rounds of challenges and disruptions, which has taught us that we have other options too.
That gave us the confidence to look at different options as Singapore learned from various things.
For example, if you recall COVID-19, we had border closures, we had supply disruptions, which got us to think about supply diversification – when it came to eggs, when it came to chickens.
It also got us thinking about whether we need to strengthen stockpiling.
And therefore, in the last Sitting, we had Parliamentary Questions (PQs) on stockpiling, and what we do with rice and what we do with chicken.
With greater options now, I am not solely reliant on local food production only.
We have about 8% out of 20% for the leafy vegetables, which we think over time, we can grow.
But overall, I would say this, that our yield production has certainly shown promise.
So, that gives very good promise in terms of whether we are able to meet the 2035 target.
Certainly, it is something that we are doing more than just aspirations, we are tracking quite carefully.
As I said, we are tracking the statistics, we are putting in programmes, schemes to ensure and help our farms transform to achieve those goals.
These, put together, give us a bit more options.
I think that is one question some people ask me all the time.

I think maybe it is not so much thinking in terms of goalpost, but maybe perhaps I am giving you a better goalkeeper that can perhaps save the day with more options or more plays or more tool kits in this playbook.
This is one way in which we can ensure food security in Singapore in terms of need.
It is not wise for us to reveal how long we can hold out with our stockpiles.

But I would like to assure the Member that this is something that we watch very closely to ensure that in times of need, in times of security, we want to attain and ensure some sort of normalcy in the short term, such that you do not feel too much of a difference, in terms of how we practise and what we eat every day.
But over time, you will need to look at other options, whether it is local food security, or by hopefully then, we are able to find options through our diversification efforts.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I want to clear as many questions as I can during this Question Time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And the same applies to the front bench answering.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Well, if the 2030 goal was a moonshot, then I think it does make sense to come back to earth and find spots that will work as well.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: On that note, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State, can you share more about our diversification strategy and which are the non-traditional countries that we have started importing more food from?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The short answer is, that is not part of this PQ, so you may want to file another PQ.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Having said that, an example would be chickens.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have seen how we have coped with the supply chain disruption during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have gone from just Malaysia to other countries, such as Brazil.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you think about eggs, we went all the way to Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I think you can find the whole list of diversified sources on the Singapore Food Agency (SFA) website too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have filed two questions for yesterday's Sitting and the Minister said that these will be addressed today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, one question regarding how will the SFA supports and transitions farms that have invested heavily in technology to meet the original target, but now, whose produce is less aligned with the new protein and fibre targets, and what enhanced grants or offtake schemes are available to assist?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have not really quite heard the answer to this question.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the Government consider going beyond one-off grants for capital expenditure and offer grants to help with operating expenditure?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And one supplementary question for my fibre question, has SFA considered whether narrowing the recognised fibre crop set, increases systemic risk, such as pest or climate vulnerability, and if so, what will be the mitigation measures?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To the Member's questions on cost and vulnerability, I think that it is something that really depends on your mode of farming.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you are dealing with traditional land farms, of course, you have got things like soil disease, you have things like pests and other things, and farm and vegetable diseases that could spread.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Where you have the extreme case where you have agri-tech farms in very controlled environments, I think that also provides a different sort of environment which helps to mitigate risks.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We find that some of our farmers have already moved in this space.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, as I mentioned earlier on, Greenphyto is one, but you have others like Green Harvest and Yili Farms, who have also done some transformations to put their crops in greenhouses, which reduces the effects of climate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And therefore, a number of our farms that we have funded out of our schemes – so not so much invested in; let me rephrase that, we did not invest in, but we funded through our schemes – have been many of these new climate-resilient farms too, which helps in terms of yield, because you have shielded yourself from the weather, as one example.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And of course, that reduces pests as well.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On other areas in which Member spoke about, including whether we will fund operating costs, I think that is always a danger down a slippery slope.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ultimately, where we want to focus on is capability building, looking at new areas in which we can support.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have a hatchery centre and a broodstock centre, which helps, for example, to get higher yields for our egg stock.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also have hatcheries that improve the quality of fingerlings, so that aquaculture can be farmed and raised with higher yields and that are stronger in terms of survivability rates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These help farms in more game-changing ways than just helping to fund the operating costs, which may continue in current modes, current forms, which are not sustainable in the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I think what we want to do, as I shared, is build new capability, new capacities and new ways of farming, which maximises yield, which helps overcomes our constraints in land and other weaknesses that we have in terms of manpower, for example, through automation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Today, for example, we are also encouraging some of our farms, whether it is aquaculture farms or even traditional agriculture farms, to go abroad, understand from some of these trends that can be found, agriculture or agri-tech type farming that you find overseas, whether it is in China or in other parts of Europe, and other areas in Asia, to which we can learn from too, in terms of how they have been able to scale, if they have been able to bring down cost of production.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are areas in which we want to learn from.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we are trying to help our farms overcome our constraints here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Senior Minister of State spoke about enhancing demand offtake.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This could be a 1% quota for major food importers and supermarkets like NTUC Fairprice and Sheng Siong.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: You can call it "1 by 30", if you would like.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: What we really want is to help our local farmers connect them through organisations such as Singapore Agro-Food Enterprises Federation Limited.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We are working very hard to connect them with many of our retailers, hoteliers, restaurant caterers – and many today are already supporting our local farms.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I spoke about Kok Fah Technology Farm, I spoke about Green Harvest, traditional farms, new farms.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think what is key is really to be competitive with the market to provide an offering that Singaporeans would consider.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I know supermarkets such as Fairprice, for example, tell me they have got a whole section dedicated just for local produce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think ultimately it is also encouraging and building awareness with our consumers that local farm produce is fresher.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we give you slightly different offerings for a slightly different premium.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I think for things like vegetables, even bean sprouts, the reason why they have a pretty good hold on the market is because consumers also want freshness and there is a segment of market that wish for that.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We hope that with helping our businesses build new capabilities, improve yields, lower their cost of production, we hope that in the long term that helps them be more competitive in the market.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope that our consumers will also be able to discern the advantages of supporting local and buying local.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On our part, whether it is through procurement, whether it is through encouraging retailers, hoteliers, I think we will continue to do our part to encourage them to buy local produce, so that we can support local farmers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is in our interest, on the record, to ensure that our local farms, our local producers thrive, progress and play a big part in our Singapore Food Story 2.
